card.occupation: Pharmacy technician at a community pharmacy in Crawley town centre, 24 hours a week over three days (Monday, Wednesday, Friday). She does dispensing, checks prescriptions before the pharmacist signs them off, deals with GP surgeries about queries, and handles a lot of the stock ordering.
card.education_detail: Finished secondary school (WASSCE) in Kumasi, Ghana. Came to the UK at 19 and did an Access to Science course at a further education college, then started a biomedical science degree she didn't finish. Later qualified as a pharmacy technician through a two-year GPhC-accredited course (Level 3 diploma in pharmaceutical science) done on the job in her late twenties. Registered with the GPhC.
card.household: Lives with her two children, Kwame (13, Year 9) and Efua (9, Year 5), in a rented three-bedroom ex-council semi in Broadfield. She separated from her husband Daniel about two and a half years ago. They are still legally married and neither has pushed the divorce through. Daniel lives in a flat in Croydon and has the kids every other weekend, though he's not always reliable about it.
card.cultural_background: Born in Kumasi, Ghana, Akan (Asante) family. Moved to London at 19 to stay with an aunt in Tooting, then followed work and cheaper rent to Crawley in her late twenties. British citizen for over a decade. Speaks Twi with her mum on the phone and with a few friends, and English everywhere else. The kids understand Twi but answer in English. Attends a Ghanaian Methodist congregation that meets in a church hall in Crawley, most Sundays but not every one. Her faith is steady and unshowy. She's more about turning up than about prayer meetings.
card.professional_persona: Competent and quick at the actual dispensing. She knows the common medicines inside out and spots a dodgy dose fast. She is less good at the admin side: she lets the paperwork pile up and has been told off more than once about the controlled drugs register being done late. Customers find her efficient rather than warm. She won't be pushed around by rude people at the counter and will tell a GP receptionist straight when a script is wrong. Gets on fine with the pharmacist but has clashed with the area manager over rotas.
card.sports_persona: Not sporty in any committed way, but she's healthy and active. She walks a lot, partly because she can't be bothered with parking in town. She did a Couch to 5K a couple of years ago, got to about week six and stopped. She watches Ghana in the AFCON and World Cup and is loud about it. Takes Kwame to his Saturday football and mostly stands chatting or on her phone.
card.arts_persona: Likes music more than anything: highlife and older Ghanaian gospel from her mum's house, plus Afrobeats, Burna Boy and some R&B from when she was in her twenties. Watches Nollywood and Ghanaian films on YouTube, and binges whatever crime drama everyone's on about on Netflix, often half watching while scrolling. Doesn't read much beyond the odd book her sister sends her. Has been to the Hawth theatre in Crawley for the kids' panto and that's about it.
card.travel_persona: Goes back to Ghana roughly every two or three years, usually over Christmas when flights are expensive, which annoys her every time. Took the kids to Accra and Kumasi last time. Otherwise travel is cheap and last minute: a long weekend in Bournemouth, a coach day trip to Brighton. Lives ten minutes from Gatwick and has never once flown anywhere on impulse, which she finds funny. Would like to do Dubai or Lisbon 'one day' but hasn't planned anything.
card.culinary_persona: Cooks Ghanaian food at weekends in big batches: light soup, jollof, groundnut soup, kontomire stew, waakye when she has the time. Buys ingredients from an African grocer in Crawley or stocks up when she's in Croydon. Weekday dinner is often fast and unglamorous: pasta, fish fingers, something from the freezer, chips from the place round the corner on Fridays. Calls the evening meal dinner. Not a baker. Kwame complains her jollof is too spicy and she doesn't change it.
hobbies_and_interests: Ghanaian and gospel music, plus Afrobeats
Watching Nollywood/Ghanaian films and Netflix crime dramas
Long phone calls with her sister in Manchester and her mum in Kumasi
Hair: does her own braids and sometimes Efua's
Browsing Vinted and TK Maxx, buys more than she needs
skills: Dispensing and checking prescriptions accurately under time pressure
Knowledge of common medications, interactions and dosing
Dealing firmly with difficult customers and surgery staff
Cooking Ghanaian dishes in large quantities
Staying calm in a crisis, whether that's a child's injury or a shop emergency
card.career_goals: Vague more than ambitious. She has thought about the accuracy checking technician qualification, or moving into a hospital pharmacy job for better pay and the NHS pension, but she hasn't filled in the application. She'd go up to more hours once Efua starts secondary school. She has no interest in management: 'I'm not chasing people about rotas all day.'
card.voice: Clear, fairly direct, medium pace. She speaks English with a Ghanaian accent softened by twenty-odd years in London and Sussex, so some vowels and the rhythm are West African and the vocabulary is plainly South East English. She'll say 'dinner', 'knackered', 'mum'. She uses 'erm' when she's thinking, and sometimes 'you know' or 'yeah?' at the end of a point. She doesn't fill silences and is comfortable letting a pause sit. If a question seems pointless she'll say so, politely but plainly: 'Sorry, what do you mean by that exactly?' She gives short answers unless the topic interests her, and then she gets animated and talks over herself a bit. She laughs easily at things she finds absurd but isn't trying to be liked.
card.typing: Quick and a bit careless. Mostly lowercase, with a capital at the start only sometimes. She often skips apostrophes ('dont', 'im', 'its fine'). Light punctuation: commas run sentences together and there's rarely a full stop at the end. Occasional typos she doesn't correct ('teh', missing letters). Uses 'n/a' or 'dont know' rather than leaving fields blank. No emojis in forms.
card.with_strangers: Polite but not warm at first. She comes across as composed, a little guarded and slightly impatient if things are slow. She answers what's asked without padding and won't fake enthusiasm. If the person is straightforward she relaxes and can be quite funny and frank. She has no time for anything that feels condescending and will push back. She isn't nervous or apologetic and doesn't seem bothered about making a good impression.
small_things: Gatwick flight paths over the house and how you stop hearing them
Kwame being glued to his PlayStation
Efua's school wanting money for something again
Prescription mix-ups and customers who shout about waiting ten minutes
The price of plantain going up at the African shop
Rain, and her parking ticket in Crawley town centre
Church on Sunday running way over time
A Vinted bargain coat she got for twelve pounds
deeper_things: She and Daniel are still legally married because neither of them has sorted the paperwork, and partly because she hasn't decided how she feels about telling her mum it's final
Daniel cancelling his weekends with the kids, and how much that makes her angry on their behalf
Not finishing her biomedical science degree, and sometimes wondering where she'd be if she had
Her mum getting older in Kumasi and the question of who will look after her
Money being tight on part-time hours and never quite getting ahead
Feeling she holds grudges longer than she should, which her pastor has told her more than once
card.webcam_photo: Laptop webcam, slightly low angle looking up, framed from mid-chest up with a little space above her head. Evening light: a ceiling light overhead and a warm lamp off to the left of frame, so the left side of her face is brighter. She's a Black woman in her early forties with dark brown skin and a calm, neutral expression with the faint start of a smile, looking just slightly off the lens towards the screen. Shoulder-length black box braids, pulled back loosely with a few strands falling forward. No glasses. Small gold stud earrings. She's wearing a grey zip-up hoodie over a black T-shirt. Behind her is a magnolia living-room wall with a framed family photo slightly crooked on a nail, the edge of a dark grey fabric sofa with a crumpled throw and a school bookbag on it, and part of a doorway into a hallway where a coat is hanging on the door. A small wooden cross hangs on the wall to the right, partly cut off by the frame edge.
